analysis.one_liner: Funds a $25 billion border wall with fees and benefit cuts targeting workers without legal status.
analysis.headline: The WALL Act, introduced January 29, 2025 with 6 Republican sponsors, sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no committee or floor action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill spends $25 billion building a barrier along the U.S.-Mexico border and pays for it by restricting tax credits and federal benefits to people with Social Security numbers authorized to work, charging a $300 fee for each person on a tax return who files with an ITIN, and imposing fines of $3,000 to $10,000 for illegal entry or reentry and $50 per month for overstaying a visa. It also requires agencies to use E-Verify to check immigration status before granting unemployment, food, and housing benefits. It was referred to the Finance Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction firms that would build the wall would receive up to $25 billion in federal money available until spent. Citizens who support stronger border enforcement would get a funded wall, and federal and state agencies would gain new tools to deny benefits to people without work authorization.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Border construction contractors and wall supporters

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $25 billion to build a physical barrier along the southern land border, with the money available until expended [S2][S3].

Restricts the child tax credit, earned income credit, and lifetime learning credit to taxpayers and children with valid Social Security numbers, excluding people prohibited from working in the U.S. [S2][S3].
Charges a $300 fee for each individual on a tax return who files using an individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN) instead of a Social Security number [S2][S3].

Sets civil fines of $3,000 to $10,000 for improper entry or reentry and $50 per month of visa overstay, plus up to 6 months' imprisonment for a first illegal entry and up to 2 years for a repeat [S2][S3].
Requires state agencies and housing programs to use E-Verify to confirm work-authorized status before granting unemployment compensation, SNAP food benefits, and federal housing assistance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers shoulder the $25 billion. Immigrant workers who file taxes without work authorization pay a $300 fee per family member and lose the child tax credit, earned income credit, and education credits, including on behalf of U.S. citizen children. Noncitizens face new fines and potential jail time, and authorized applicants for food and housing benefits face an added E-Verify check that can delay or wrongly deny aid.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and immigrant families filing with ITINs

drawbacks.text: The child tax credit change hits mixed-status families: a parent with an ITIN would lose the credit for a U.S. citizen child who has a Social Security number, because the taxpayer's own number no longer counts as valid [S3].

The $300-per-person ITIN fee is effectively a tax on low-wage workers who file returns without work authorization, and the credit exclusions withdraw refunds from workers who pay into payroll taxes [S2][S3].

The $25 billion is mandatory spending available until expended with no expiration or cap on final cost, and the offsets have no stated dollar value, so the wall could cost more than the fees and fines raise [S2][S3].

Requiring E-Verify checks for food and housing benefits adds an administrative step that can delay or incorrectly deny aid to work-authorized applicants due to database errors — a cost honest supporters of verification would need to manage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a concrete, funded enforcement project and new penalties, which its supporters view as worth the money. The costs fall narrowly: families with an unauthorized parent lose thousands of dollars a year in refundable credits for citizen children, workers without status pay a new filing fee, and taxpayers fund $25 billion whose offsets are not quantified. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much one values the wall; the burden falls almost entirely on low-income immigrant families rather than broadly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on January 29, 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Katie Britt introduced the bill in the Senate on January 29, 2025, where it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
Five Republican senators — Cruz, Risch, Barrasso, Rounds, and Wicker — cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps: no committee markup, no vote, and no floor action since the January 2025 referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet. Mixed-status families keep their current tax credits and ITIN filers avoid the $300 fee for now, while wall supporters have gained nothing beyond introduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mixed-status families keep credits for now

for.name: Sen. Katie Britt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the WALL Act of 2025 and arranged five Senate Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 5 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Cruz, Risch, Barrasso, Rounds, Wicker)

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the January 29, 2025 referral — no markup, vote, or floor scheduling in the months since.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill has drawn no Democratic action in committee.

industries.note: A $25 billion mandatory appropriation, available until expended, would flow to firms building the barrier. Whether that money serves ordinary people depends on how much one values the wall; the funds come from taxpayers and from fees on low-income immigrant workers [S2][S3].

The bill adds jail terms of up to 6 months for a first illegal entry and up to 2 years for a repeat, which would increase demand for detention capacity, much of it supplied by private prison companies. Their gain comes from more people imprisoned [S3].

analysis.trajectory: With a handful of Republican cosponsors, no Democratic support, and no Finance Committee action in the months since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress; most bills at this stage die when the session ends.
